newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai central bank curbs foreign fund inflows.
newsitem.headline: Thai central bank curbs foreign fund inflows.

text.p: The Bank of Thailand on Friday put limits on short-term loans that offshore banking units bring in for relending to Thai-based clients.

A central bank circular said it requested Thai-based offshore banking units to exercise greater scrutiny in approving out-in loans, saying special favour should be given to clients engaged in exports and related business.

It said short-term foreign loans for activities that contribute little to economic growth, including those for wasteful consumer spending, market speculation, and for arbitrage on high Thai interest rates should be discouraged.
Out-in loans refer to foreign funds that offshore banks import for relending to local clients.

The central bank circular said the rise of out-in loans extended by offshore banking units during September-December this year is limited to seven percent of the increase of baht-denominated loans they lend out over the same period.

It said any out-in loan increase above the seven percent limit would be permitted only if offshore banking units extend additional out-out loans on a respective ratio of five to one during the same period.
Out-out loans are foreign funds brought in for processing by Thai-based banks which relend them to borrowers in third countries.
The circular said the central bank raised to $5 million from $2 million the minimum out-in loan that licensed offshore banking units can extend to new local clients, effective December 1, 1996.
The central bank measures were aimed at curbing inflows of short-term foreign funds after their rapid increase early this year.

The sharp rise of inflows of offshore funds has raised concerns among market analysts that Thailand could face serious financial shocks semilar to the Mexico crisis in early 1995 if foreign funds were pulled out on short notice.
Central bank statistics said foreign debts of the Thai private sector rose to $66.2 billion at end-1995 from $25.1 billion at end-1991.
